NVDA.supply_chain_summary: NVIDIA sits at the apex of the AI compute supply chain as a fabless semiconductor company, designing the world's most sought-after GPUs and accelerators while depending critically on TSMC for cutting-edge fabrication and SK Hynix for HBM memory supply. Its downstream customer base is dominated by the largest global hyperscalers and cloud providers, who are racing to build AI infrastructure and collectively account for the majority of NVIDIA's explosive data center revenue growth.

upstream.name: Qualcomm Inc.
upstream.relationship: Supplier of 5G modem chipsets for iPhone lineup (transitioning to in-house)

AAPL.supply_chain_summary: Apple sits at the apex of a highly complex global supply chain, acting as a 'fabless' designer that orchestrates hundreds of specialized suppliers — most critically TSMC for advanced chip fabrication — while distributing finished products primarily through carrier partnerships and its own retail ecosystem. Its downstream relationships are uniquely diversified across direct consumers, telecom carriers, and platform partners (notably Google), with Services revenue increasingly reducing dependence on any single hardware distribution channel.

upstream.name: Applied Materials Inc.

MU.supply_chain_summary: Micron Technology sits at the heart of the global memory supply chain as one of only three major DRAM manufacturers (alongside Samsung and SK Hynix) and a leading NAND producer, making it critically dependent on a concentrated set of semiconductor equipment suppliers — particularly ASML, Applied Materials, and Lam Research — for its capital-intensive fabrication processes. On the demand side, Micron is increasingly exposed to AI infrastructure buildout through surging HBM shipments to NVIDIA and server DRAM demand from hyperscalers, while maintaining diversified end-market exposure across mobile, automotive, and client computing.

ARM.supply_chain_summary: ARM Holdings sits at a uniquely asset-light position in the semiconductor supply chain — it neither fabricates nor sells physical chips, but instead licenses CPU and GPU IP to virtually every major semiconductor company and OEM in the industry, making it a foundational upstream intellectual property provider. Its revenue is driven almost entirely by licensing fees and per-unit royalties from downstream customers spanning mobile, data center, automotive, and IoT markets, giving it extraordinary leverage but also high concentration risk among a handful of large licensees like Apple, Qualcomm, and MediaTek.

MRVL.supply_chain_summary: Marvell Technology sits at a critical juncture in the data infrastructure supply chain, designing custom and merchant silicon solutions — including ethernet, storage, and custom AI ASICs — that depend heavily on TSMC's advanced foundry nodes and third-party EDA/IP providers. Its downstream exposure is increasingly concentrated in hyperscale cloud providers (Amazon, Google, Microsoft), which now represent the dominant growth engine through custom ASIC co-design programs, alongside traditional networking and storage OEM customers.
